meta.title: Czech B1
meta.subtitle: 1,000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Czech → English (see the Czech, recall the meaning) and English → Czech (see an English meaning, recall the Czech). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,000 words and expressions for level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no Czech exam board publishes a word list beyond A2 — the A1 and A2 decks follow the official list of the permanent-residence exam, but the B1 citizenship exam and Charles University's CCE exams publish none. So 292 of the 1,000 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the fourteen themes of the Council of Europe's Threshold Level (van Ek and Trim, 1990), the specification the CEFR's level B1 descends from: personal identification, house and home and the environment, daily life, free time and entertainment, travel, relations with other people, health and body care, education, shopping, food and drink, services, places, language and the weather — the next layer of vocabulary beyond A1 and A2 — together with the words of opinion and argument the level needs. They are Folio's choice, not an exam board's, and this is not an official word list. The other 708 are the commonest words of everyday Czech not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. No word taught in A1 or A2 is repeated. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 7 multi-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Czech changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 492 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 268 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for já (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's present forms being its future. 31 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. 2 pronouns show their cases. Real example sentences come with 955 of the 1,000 words, three apiece for 851, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
